Newly settled juveniles of Margaritifera laevis emerge from the gills of their salmonid host at a shell length of only 0.03 centimeters , marking the transition from the parasitic glochidium stage to an independent, filter-feeding existence. This minute size at settlement is typical for freshwater pearl mussels and reflects an energetic strategy that prioritises high fecundity over investment in individual offspring. The initial post-settlement period is a critical bottleneck, as the tiny bivalves must immediately begin filtering phytoplankton and organic detritus from the interstitial water. Growth during the first few years is exceedingly slow, with individuals taking over a decade to approach reproductive maturity. Field studies conducted in northern Japan have documented that the average age at which these mussels first become capable of reproduction is approximately 13 years, at which point they have attained a shell length near 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters]. This delayed maturation is consistent with the prolonged juvenile phase observed in other Margaritifera species and is thought to be an adaptation to the cold, oligotrophic streams that constitute their primary habitat. The energetic demands of gametogenesis are not initiated until the shell has reached this substantial size threshold.

Reproductive output in Margaritifera laevis is remarkably high, compensating for the intense mortality faced by larvae and early juveniles. Adult females release glochidia into the water column, where they must attach to the gills of a suitable host fish, typically a salmonid. The maximum number of glochidia produced per day by a single female has been estimated at roughly 22,000 larvae per day [Ri = roughly 22,000 larvae per day] under optimal thermal conditions of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This extraordinary daily fecundity is a life-history strategy that offsets the extremely low probability that any given glochidium will successfully encounter and infect a host. The reproductive period is synchronised with the summer warming of the water, ensuring that glochidia are released when young-of-the-year salmonid parr are most abundant. The total seasonal output from a large, old female can therefore number in the millions, a necessity given the narrow window for host infection. Such high reproductive rates are typical of unionid mussels that rely on a parasitic larval stage.

The maximum body size attained by Margaritifera laevis is substantial, with the largest documented individuals reaching an ultimate shell length of 13.3 centimeters [Li = 13.3 centimeters]. Associated with this considerable shell length is a correspondingly large soft-tissue mass; the asymptotic wet weight of a fully grown adult is estimated to be 84.7 grams [Wwi = 84.7 grams]. This mass is achieved only after many decades of slow, continuous growth, reflecting the low metabolic rates and stable environmental conditions in the cold, well-oxygenated rivers this species inhabits. The relationship between shell length and body mass follows a power law, and the value for this species is consistent with allometric equations derived for other freshwater bivalves. Such a large body size confers several advantages, including increased filtering capacity, greater fecundity, and enhanced resistance to predation by muskrats and otters. However, the energy investment required to build and maintain this biomass over a lifespan that can exceed several decades is considerable. The species' exceptionally slow growth rate limits its ability to recover from population disturbances.

The embryonic development of Margaritifera laevis begins within the marsupial gills of the female, where fertilised eggs are brooded over the winter months. Upon release from the brood chamber, the free-swimming glochidia are approximately 0.02 centimeters [Lb = approximately 0.02 centimeters] in shell length at the time of their release from the parent, a dimension characteristic of the parasitic larval stage. The age of the newly hatched glochidia at the point of their emergence from the female is 10 days [ab = 10 days] after fertilisation when brooded at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the typical thermal regime in early spring. These microscopic larvae are lecithotrophic, relying entirely on yolk reserves as they drift in the current and attempt to attach to a passing fish. The short duration of this free-living stage means that successful host infection is critically dependent on the synchronous presence of both larvae and susceptible fish hosts. The small size of the glochidia facilitates their passive dispersal and their ability to lodge within the gill filaments of the host.

Longevity in Margaritifera laevis is exceptional among freshwater bivalves, with individuals capable of surviving for many decades under natural conditions. The maximum lifespan of this species has been recorded at 67 years [am = 67 years] in natural populations when water temperatures average 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a value that aligns with the extreme longevity documented for other members of the Margaritiferidae family. This remarkable lifespan is accompanied by a very slow rate of senescence, with old individuals showing minimal evidence of physiological decline in their filtering capacity or reproductive output. The species' persistence in cold, nutrient-poor waters may contribute to its extended longevity by reducing metabolic wear and tear. The shell itself serves as an archive of environmental conditions, with annual growth rings allowing researchers to reconstruct historical stream temperatures and water quality. Such extreme lifespans have significant implications for conservation, as the loss of a single cohort of adults represents an irreplaceable loss of decades of reproductive potential. Margaritifera laevis thus stands as a testament to the extreme slow-life-history extreme within the Bivalvia.
